entries.title: More sex, different endings: how fan fiction makes our dreams come true
entries.summary: From Heated Rivalry to Harry Potter, popular series are inspiring fan fiction read by thousands online. Now the authors of those online works are getting publishing deals of their ownShortly after this year’s London book fair, rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 201
entries.content:
Shortly after this year’s London book fair, rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027.

This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide.

The appeal for publishers seems obvious enough. The best loved works of fan fiction (or “fics”, as they are known), many of which are multi-chapter epics running to hundreds of thousands of words, are published online, chapter by chapter, to a passionate and hyper-connected audience of readers. Not only do these works inevitably retain echoes of the much-loved creations on which they are based, they also bring with them a ready-made audience, bound by their love of the urtext and buoyed up by the pleasures of collective obsession. Some fics become so popular they beget fandoms of their own, generating fan fiction, fan art and even translations into other languages.

If you have never read a word of fan fiction, if you have never stayed up into the early hours searching for Buffy the Vampire Slayer fics (Buffy/Faith for ever and always), you might be wondering: what could possibly possess thousands of people with jobs, friends and families to spend hours of their time writing stories based on other stories, and hundreds of thousands more to read them? What is drawing a whole new generation of fans to fan fiction through the gateway drug of gay ice-hockey romance Heated Rivalry, with tens of thousands of fics published on Archive of Our Own, and thousands more for the Game Changers book series on which the TV show is based? The answer is simple enough: fan fiction is the cheapest and most easily customisable medium of cultural wish fulfilment.

As a quick glance at any fan fiction platform will tell you, it seems that when you love a particular cultural product, you tend to wish there was more sex in it. Maybe the product itself is sexy in its own right, the chemistry (on screen or on paper) overt and undeniable. Maybe there’s just a hint of sexual tension, or none at all, but a wealth of deeply drawn characters upon which your fandom can project its own most fervent desires. What do you do when you cannot personally strong-arm the author to write a sequel in which your two favourite characters finally give in to the feelings you have long suspected them of harbouring? What do you do when you have neither the time nor the resources to single-handedly script, cast, shoot, produce and professionally edit another season in which the warrior princess and her plucky sidekick finally get together? You turn to fan fiction.

There are other, more obvious, wishes that fan fiction is uniquely equipped to fulfil. You might love a story so much you wish you could be in it. Well, you can be if you’ve got the time and inclination to write fan fiction; all you have to do is include a “self-insert” (or a “Mary Sue”, as they are sometimes less charitably known). You might love everything about a story but wish it had ended differently. Good news! You can write your preferred ending yourself, unless someone else in your fandom has got there first, in which case, even better news! You can have all the satisfaction with none of the work.

At the most basic level, when you love something as much as fandoms love the things they love, you really just wish there was more of it. But to understand why fan fiction matters so much to so many people, we need to look at how it works. The extreme familiarity of the worlds in which fan fiction is set allows for a kind of emotional shorthand, which in turn lets fans play within the bounds of that familiarity or push well beyond it, reimagining scenes and characters and storylines in ways that can be deeply resonant. Not by accident is so much fan fiction queer, regardless of how queer-coded or not the source material may be. And how else to explain the popularity of some of the more dramatic subcategories that exist within fan fiction? There are hurt/comfort fics, where a character suffers deep emotional or physical trauma and is comforted by another character; or “character death” fics, where a character dies and everyone is really, really sad about it; or that wonderful catch-all “angst”, in its many permutations (“‘light angst”, “heavy angst”, “angst and smut”, “angst with a happy ending”) … When you’re reading fan fiction, you’re invested before you’ve even seen the first word. This makes for a very specific reading experience: it’s reading for emotional gratification. It’s instant, it’s cathartic, and it leaves you wanting more. And all of this material is created and made available for free, with (at least in theory) no motivation other than a shared love of the original work that started it all off.

But as the monetisation of fan fiction continues apace, the inevitable backlash and soul-searching have begun. Specific to the Harry Potter fandom is a discomfort with the possibility that even fan fiction rewritten as original fiction might draw new readers to the books themselves, helping JK Rowling to bankroll what many see as a campaign against transgender rights. More generally, there is a sense that in its desire to make the most of the fan fiction bandwagon, the publishing industry is rerouting opportunities that might otherwise have gone to first-time writers of original fiction. And on a philosophical level, the commercial prospecting of fan fiction feels to some like a betrayal of the very essence of the form. Fan fiction is supposed to be a labour of love – not just for those who write it, but for those who read it, too (for not every fic is a masterpiece, and much clumsy prose must be endured). What will become of fan fiction if people start writing it in the hope they might someday be able to sell their work to a publisher? How will that influence the kinds of things they write, and their relationship with the online communities on whose support they depend?

Already there are signs of some of the difficulties that plague traditional publishing, such as allegations of AI use, and a preoccupation with “reader engagement”. Meanwhile, in a turn of events that may seem – to the more fatalistically inclined – like a harbinger of endtimes, AO3 was recently taken down for more than two weeks as a result of a “security incident”. The website is more or less back up now, but the internet’s reactions during its downtime, ranging from the tongue-in-cheek to the genuinely distressed, demonstrate one thing: people need their fan fiction. Publishing trends come and go, but fan fiction in its many incarnations – from the re-imagined myths of Ovid’s Metamorphoses to 1960s Star Trek fanzines, to the present day – has been around for ever. As long as there are stories, books, movies and TV shows, there will be fandoms. And as long as there are fandoms, there will be fan fiction.

First Summer by Ekin Oklap is published by Summit. To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
entries.summary: The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delightAs veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive abou
entries.content:
As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along.

The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation.

In Britain, Q magazine seemed to publish one every other issue: not just the 100 Best Albums of All Time (three times in the space of nine years), but the 100 Greatest British Albums, the 100 Greatest Songs of All Time, the 1001 Songs You Must Own, the 100 Greatest Singers, the 100 Greatest Guitar Tracks Ever, the 100 Best Albumsof the 90s, the 100 Greatest Stars of the 20th Century. In a very American bit of supersizing, Rolling Stone magazine – which had first printed an 100 best albums list in 1987 – dramatically upped the ante by expanding their best-ever lists from a mere 100 entries to 500.

You might have thought the public’s appetite for all this had been satiated to the point of nausea, but clearly not. The listicle remains an almost foolproof way of attracting attention (full disclosure: I compile the Guardian’s fortnightly Ranked lists of the best tracks by a given artist, and they’re almost invariably among the most-read music features on the paper’s website). Presumably imbued with a certain if-you-can’t-beat-them spirit, Wyman – whose CV includes the New Yorker, the New York Times, Rolling Stone and a stint at NPR: no fly-by-night hack he – has taken it upon himself to apply a certain rigour to the enterprise. His lists, initially published by New York Magazine and Vulture, involve ranking the entirety of a given artist’s catalogue, weaving context and biography among the judgments to provide a neat career overview. That this is obviously a fairly mammoth undertaking is underlined by the sheer length of the print version: rating every song from the oeuvres of seven artists – the Beatles, Michael Jackson, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd, the Eagles, the Clash and Nirvana – it weighs in at around 500 pages.

Wyman is a good writer. You can take issue with his opinions, which are expressed in time-honoured loudmouth US rock-crit style (indeed, taking issue with his opinions is part of the point, to which end I’ll just note his belief that the Beatles’ I’ll Cry Instead is a better song than Yesterday, Come Together, I Feel Fine, Taxman and We Can Work It Out is frankly insane and leave it at that). But you’d have a harder time finding fault with his turn of phrase, which is pithy and incisive in equal measure. The steroidal thunder of Good Times Bad Times, the opening track on Led Zeppelin’s debut album, is evidence “the terms of the debate had been changed” – an impressively succinct description of the band’s impact amid the more measured practitioners of the late 60s-blues revival. His line about the Beatles’ Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da – “the whimsy will continue until morale improves” – isn’t just snarky, but a very neat summation of the song’s chief failing: for all its ostensible jollity, it doesn’t sound like anyone involved in its manufacture was enjoying themselves very much.

As a biographer, Wyman is very good at finding a minor but telling detail (the similarities between Michael Jackson’s latter-day cocktail of grandstanding and self-pity and the approach to public life of Donald Trump; the lack of contemporary respect afforded Led Zeppelin summarised by a 1975 Playboy magazine poll in which John Bonham was voted the 12th best drummer in the world, behind Karen Carpenter) and as a critic, he’s possessed of a perspective that’s often intriguingly original. He views Nirvana’s Nevermind not as an explosion of generational angst, but a straightforward breakup album, fuelled by Kurt Cobain’s split from former girlfriend Tobi Vail; he locks into a line from overlooked Clash B-side The Prisoner – which depicts suburbanites “hanging out the washing, cutting coupons and generally being decent” – as evidence of an empathy frequently lacking amid punk’s penchant for outraging the squares.

The final part of the book, which ranks every inductee to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, is the least satisfying – partly because no one outside the US really gives a monkey’s about the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, and partly because Wyman’s approach becomes quite spectacularly crabby, taking issue with 75% of the inductees, from Black Sabbath (“their reputation and lingering image always transcended their actual work”) to Abba (“not a band that left much of a mark on history”) to Laura Nyro (“second-rate”) to Gene Vincent (“too fresh faced”) to Bill Withers (“not a person of particular substance” – thank you, Lady Bracknell) while lobbying instead for the inclusion of – wait for it – KC and the Sunshine Band.

Of course, this is the kind of contrarianism that’s guaranteed to get clicks, which brings us to one minor problem with Wyman’s approach, directly linked to his lists’ original online context: the creeping sense that he knows rather too well that an outraged response is just as likely to send a feature viral as one of gushing delight, and is occasionally engaged in the business of just saying things for effect. There doubtless are people who genuinely believe that the Velvet Underground were “pretentious and quite often unlistenable”, but you somehow don’t believe Wyman is one of them: he just knows that someone sharing a link in a fury is still sharing a link.

Still, this is a minor criticism of a book that offers a convincing explanation for the rock list’s apparently eternal popularity: even at its most contrarian and infuriating, it’s still entertaining; at its best, it’s genuinely illuminating.

entries.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
entries.summary: A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independenceIn the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the i
entries.content:
In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud.

Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence.

Adder Stone opens with a group of men emptying the Jones family home, boxes of treasured possessions roughly carried out, items of furniture unceremoniously dumped in the middle of the driveway and left “huddled together like mourners at the wrong funeral”. The digger then moves in and, with just a few violent sweeps of its yellow claw, razes the house to rubble and dust. This act of destruction is a source of profound grief for the family’s patriarch Dai, as well as for his sensitive teenage son, Emyr. But for Olwen, wife and mother, it presents a chance for a “fresh start, away from the bad memories, all the bitterness and rage”. In short, she declares: “I was free.”

What seems to follow, then, is a story of female emancipation. We learn of Olwen’s impoverished upbringing; of the illegitimate pregnancy that only added further shame to her outcast status. After they married, we learn how Olwen struggled to navigate Dai’s erratic temper and her mother-in-law’s open hostility; five years after the old woman’s death, we are told she still “hung about the place like washing on a wet day”.

But now, thanks to The Worshipful Corporation of Liverpool, Olwen has a new place, a new house to call her own. For the first time she also takes up work outside the home – a cleaning gig that comes with a pay cheque and the use of a Jeep (she quickly enlists Emyr to teach her how to drive). The cottage she cleans is rented by two Englishmen, a famous painter and his photographer friend, and here Olwen encounters a different kind of life: a life of art and music and poetry. It is, she thinks, “like someone had opened a door”.

Emyr, however, does not approve of his mother playing servant to these English employers. He warns: “By doing their dirty work you’re accepting their tyranny. You’re colluding in our suppression.” He is parroting his father’s patriotism, but also the mounting local sentiment, the air full of “mutterings about freedom fighters and a Welsh IRA”. The reservoir sparks angry protests and acts of vandalism, which tend increasingly towards violence, such that the novel’s second half becomes less about Olwen’s emancipation and more about her growing anxiety regarding her son’s radicalisation to the nationalist cause.

Clark has clearly done her research. Key dates, events, newspaper headlines – even entire articles – are mapped out here, and undoubtedly this is fascinating stuff. At times, though, it can grow somewhat overwhelming as we hurtle through huge swathes of material. Character development also feels a little rushed – the two Englishmen abruptly morph into pantomime villains. Similarly, Dai seems almost comedically unpleasant throughout and yet, upon his death, Olwen blindsides the reader by declaring: “I had spent so much of our life together wanting to be somewhere else. It was too late to realise that he was the place where I belonged.”

At its best, the mother-son relationship that gives Adder Stone its heart is tenderly drawn. Meanwhile, the descriptions of the Welsh countryside are beautiful, as we feel keenly the connection between this community and their land. Clark’s author’s note also foregrounds the connection between the novel’s events and our present moment, “as nationalism burgeons, polarisation deepens and the rhetoric grows ever angrier and more frightening”. Like an abandoned village that has lain under water only to be unearthed, so too has Clark revealed this lesser known corner of history.

entries.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
entries.summary: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagineWhen Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen t
entries.content:
When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

The work of Freud still dominates the public and medical imagination here, even though there are important ways in which he was wrong. Freud proposed that quite dramatic physical symptoms can arise as a result of repression, where the memory of an upsetting experience is pushed into the unconscious, leaving a sort of free-floating emotional energy. He saw the mind as being like a pneumatic device: emotions represented energy and that energy had to go somewhere, often leading to the development of a physical symptom.

These days, psychologists are more sceptical about this, but the influence of Freudian psychology lives on in the way we talk about psychosomatic illness – a condition where there’s no damage or disease, but clear impairment nonetheless. The terms “conversion” and “somatisation” are derived directly from Freud and still pop up frequently in the literature.

Their use is a stark reminder of the fact that, when it comes to explanations, our language can lead us astray. Importantly, the words conversion and somatisation strongly imply an active, even deliberate, process; that the patient with a psychosomatic illness is doing something that brings their symptoms about. They are converting their distress into paralysis, or somatising their sadness into pain. Is that how things really are?

There is still much to be explained about how, in the absence of damage or disease, a body can produce a symptom as dramatic as paralysis or a seizure-like episode. But we are beginning to understand what seems to be important in getting these experiences going.

First, remember that our bodies often respond to acute distress in dramatic ways. Strong emotion can entail so called tonic immobility, in which motor areas in the brain are inhibited, and voluntary movement prevented. More familiarly, it can induce trembling, speechlessness and confusion, all of which resemble neurological symptoms. Our perception of these experiences is important. Recognising strong emotion for what it is makes it more manageable. If I tremble while understanding that I am afraid, I might give myself time for the fear to pass and my nervous system to settle down.

But when these feelings are taken as a potential sign of disease, we tend to become anxious, with consequences for how we experience and attend to our bodies. Fear increases pain, so any feeling that there is bodily damage (a frightening idea) can be enough to turn up the perceptual volume on physical discomfort or unusual sensations. Paying attention to and trying to control a shaking limb will tend to increase the trembling; attending to a difficulty with movement is likely to increase how severe we think the problem is. What might have started small becomes amplified.

People vary in terms of how easy they find it to identify emotions. The term “alexithymia” (translatable as something like “no words for emotions”) refers to a difficulty with labelling and distinguishing feelings. It can range from a near full-on emotion “blindness” to a coarser grain of emotional experience, with distinctions only between, say, feeling “good” and feeling “bad”. It is not uncommon for people with psychosomatic illnesses to report that they struggle to identify emotional states.

What this could point to is that psychosomatic illnesses arise not because of what a patient is doing with their emotions, but because of what they have not been able to do with them. When we label our emotions, when we allow them to find their expression, we are allowing ourselves to know more fully what we are feeling and what we need. In a clear departure from the Freud-inspired model, it’s not that patients with these problems are “converting” their emotions into something else. It’s that they aren’t always registering them as emotions in the first place. Instead, they’re interpreted as something having gone wrong with the body, beginning a vicious cycle of anxious attention.

This is still an uncertain area of clinical practice. Emotion is not the whole picture, but it is important for understanding why some people find themselves with otherwise unexplained symptoms. For example, one way of thinking about non-epileptic seizures (a deeply distressing and disabling experience with all the hallmarks of a seizure, but without any of the expected electrical anomalies in the brain) is that they might start off with physiological elements of a panic attack – the muscular tension and the involuntary movement – but without the accompanying subjective feeling of dread; “panic without panic”.

Diego found it helpful to consider that his symptoms could be rooted in bodily expressions of anxiety and physical overload. He was a determined and upbeat guy who had taken on a second and third job to support his children financially. He had studiously avoided engaging with the possibility that this might be getting to be too much. His symptoms showed him his limits.

Psychosomatic illness is sometimes dismissed as being “all in the mind”, but this gets things back to front. When our emotions get wrapped up with physical symptoms, they are very real – “all in the body”, in fact. Bringing our emotions into our minds by thinking about them, and heeding the needs they represent, can be an important step in finding relief.

Huw Green is a clinical psychologist working in neuropsychology

Further reading

The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk (Penguin, £14.99)

It’s All in Your Head by Suzanne O’Sullivan (Vintage, £12.99)

Into the Abyss by Anthony David (Oneworld, £9.99).

entries.title: Rivals author Jilly Cooper accused of ‘extensive and deliberate plagiarism’
entries.summary: Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporariesJilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and Th
entries.content:
Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.

The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey.

According to a report in the Observer, Cooper, who died last October, committed “what appears to be extensive and deliberate plagiarism” by lifting at least 35 passages from The Serial alone.

McFadden’s daughter, Caroline McFadden, told the publication: “To steal her work so extensively and to profit off it is unconscionable.”

She said she was considering legal action, saying: “It absolutely boils my blood to think of someone stealing my mother’s work because I know how hard she worked at her craft.

“I will be looking at legal options as this can’t be allowed to stand. I sincerely hope that all of Dame Cooper’s work will be scrutinised to see if this was a pattern of hers and other talented authors’ work stolen.”

Cooper, who has sold more than 11m copies of her books in the UK alone, was given a damehood in the 2024 new year honours list for her services to literature and charity.

Disney+ is currently airing the second series of Rivals, the award-winning television adaptation of her most famous work. The show combines TV industry intrigue and racy sex scenes against the backdrop of the Cotswolds countryside in the fictional guise of Rutshire.

In its investigation, the Observer detailed 15 allegedly plagiarised passages from The Serial, which was first published from late 1975 as a weekly serialisation in a US newspaper before it was released as a book in May 1977.

In The Serial, McFadden, who died in 2024, created the off-and-on-again couple Kate and Harvey Holroyd, two progressives in California’s Marin County. The Observer noted several similarities with the dialogue in Cooper’s character, Berenice, an American feminist.

In The Serial, Kate says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open, loving relationship, based on growth and trust and sharing, and Harvey wanted his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we just weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

In Prudence, Berenice says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open living relationship based on trust and growth, and all he wanted was his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

The publication also cited another example from The Serial in which Harvey was offered lifestyle advice. The passage said: “Cut out the nine-to-five shit, Harv. You gotta get in touch with the universe. That’s the first step.”

In Prudence, Berenice offered similar advice. “You ought to cut out that nine to five shit … And get in touch with the universe.”

The Observer said it began looking at Prudence after a reader pointed out similarities with a scene in Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair.

The publication alleged that Cooper “lifts directly” from chapter 22 of the novel “both in narrative architecture and in line-by-line choice of words”. Tey died in 1952 and left no heirs.

Cooper is said to have praised The Serial for its parody of the modern feminist in a 1982 Mail on Sunday column. She said she was “tremendously comforted” when she “came across a passage in the novel The Serial by Cyra McFadden, a marvellously funny send-up of American trendies in the late seventies”.

An inquest held last year concluded that Cooper suffered a fatal head injury in a fall at her Gloucestershire home. She was found by family on 4 October 2025 and died in hospital the following day.

The Guardian has contacted Cooper’s agent, Felicity Blunt at Curtis Brown, and her publisher, Penguin, for comment. The Observer said both had declined to provide a comment.

entries.title: Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days
entries.summary: Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time overLife starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambit
entries.content:
Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter.

The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do.

Years after I left Middle-earth, the three weeks occupied by my first reading of 2666 (the longest book I’ve read multiple times) became an ongoing logistical challenge: how could I dispense with parenting, my office job and sleep as quickly as possible, so that I could immerse myself again in that torrent of words?

Hopefully some of the choices below will exert a similar pull on you. I’ve set the minimum page count at 600 – long enough that you’ll probably spend at least a week with them, quite possibly several. Books originally or usually published as separate volumes don’t qualify, so no Lord of the Rings, In Search of Lost Time, Septology or The Man Without Qualities. And, in the way of such lists, your own personal favourite is probably, scandalously, absent. But here are 20 novels that will define your life for a chunk of time, and might just change it for ever.

2666 by Roberto Bolaño (2004)

Knowing he was dying, Bolaño planned to publish the five-part novel 2666 in separate volumes, which he thought would be more financially rewarding for his family. His executors went against his wishes, the monumental 900-page book becoming a sensation first in Spanish then in Natasha Wimmer’s English translation. The novel brings the fictional Mexican border city of Santa Teresa, and its horrific wave of femicides, to large-scale and unforgettable life: it is a monstrous, irresistible vortex in which cops, serial killers, academics and a mysterious German novelist all find ends of one kind or another.

Middlemarch by George Eliot (1871-2)

Voted No 1 in the Guardian’s 100 best novels of all time poll earlier this year, Middlemarch is one of those “everything” books that, to quote Adam Mars-Jones on Ulysses, “swallowed me whole” when I read it. Eliot began a novel about a provincial doctor, abandoned it to write something quick about a character called Dorothea Brooke, and ended up combining the two into an utterly singular and unforgettable work. Perhaps its true brilliance lies in its being both a deeply enjoyable account of the varied fortunes of its large cast of characters, and a profound philosophical exploration of the nature of reality.

Dhalgren by Samuel R Delany (1975)

The story of a young man – “Kid” – becoming a poet and having a breakdown in a semi-ruined American city called Bellona, the million-selling Dhalgren is one of the stranger and more opaque science-fiction novels – and definitely the most modernist – to have found a mass audience. A circular text, it moves between plot and plotlessness, variant versions of itself, and repetitious bursts of seemingly pointless sex and violence. One to surrender to rather than conquer, the book’s draw is its extraordinary all-enveloping weirdness.

Villette by Charlotte Brontë (1853)

Written after the deaths of her siblings Emily, Anne and Patrick, Villette is the weirdest, bleakest, most puzzling of Charlotte Brontë’s novels, and my favourite by some distance. Lucy Snowe finds not only work as a schoolteacher in Villette (a fictionalised Brussels, where Brontë had taught in her 20s), but also ghosts, mental derangement and unrequited love. It features one of the great ambiguous endings in literature, what Brontë referred to as “a little puzzle”, supplied when her father objected to her original ending in which she summarily dispatched Lucy’s lover in a shipwreck.

Darkmans by Nicola Barker (2007)

An epic set in the “geographical plughole” that is Ashford, Kent, Darkmans encompasses the Channel tunnel, drug dealing, salad phobias, samurai swords, the spectre of history, and the much less metaphorical spectre of John Scogin, Edward IV’s court jester. Barker’s antic novel, which was shortlisted for the Booker prize, runs to more than 800 pages of twitchy invention, relentless as – but much funnier than – a burst water main.

It by Stephen King (1986)

By my count, King has written 17 novels that would qualify for this list, three of them longer than 1,000 pages. It isn’t just one of his longest novels, but arguably his best. Terrifying from the off, when Georgie Denbrough chases after his paper boat in an autumn storm and encounters Pennywise the clown, it also memorably evokes childhood friendship and, in the town of Derry, plunges into the dark side of American history: crime, racial and sexual bigotry, economic downturn and industrial pollution.

The Magic Mountain by Thomas Mann (1924)

Mann began this novel in 1913, intending a comic counterpart to his tragic novella Death in Venice. He completed it more than a decade later, by which time his political outlook had entirely changed, the first world war had reshaped Europe, and the book had become a philosophical meditation on time, European civilisation and the conflict between liberal humanism and rightwing reaction. Set in a tuberculosis sanatorium, it’s also one of the great books about the terror and seduction of illness.

A Brief History of Seven Killings by Marlon James (2014)

“The problem with a book,” notes one of the 75 characters in A Brief History of Seven Killings, “is that you never know what it’s planning to do to you until you’re too far into it.” What James’s Booker-prize-winning novel is planning to do is completely take over your life until you’re done with it, or it’s done with you. The attempted assassination of Bob Marley is the focal point, but the book’s braided streams of consciousness carry us from Kingston’s ghettoes to CIA plots to America’s crack epidemic.

Lies and Sorcery by Elsa Morante (1948)

When Natalia Ginzburg, then an editor at the Italian publishing house Einaudi, received the manuscript of this debut novel, she read it in a day. For decades available in English only in a bowdlerised edition, 200 pages shy of its original length, the book was restored in a new translation by Jenny McPhee in 2023. This was thanks largely to repeated praise from Elena Ferrante, who said that this portrait of the artist as a young woman showed her “what literature can be”.

Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell by Susanna Clarke (2004)

The world of Clarke’s richly imagined debut is a familiar one: the Regency England we encounter in Jane Austen novels. But in this version of it, magic, which is real but long fallen into disuse, is making a comeback. The conflict between the two magicians of the title – one conservative, the other willing to engage with powerful and treacherous forces – is involving, but the real pleasure of this book lies in the texture of its world; some of the most enchanting and playful moments lie in its footnotes.

The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton (2013)

Aged 28, Catton became the youngest writer ever to win the Booker prize, and The Luminaries – all 832 pages of it – the longest book to be so honoured. A tale of theft, murder, ghosts and desire in a New Zealand goldrush town, the book is an ever-shifting puzzle, an ingenious astrological mechanism that constantly repositions its characters and events in relation to one another. As Robert Macfarlane, chair of the Booker judges, said: it’s “as intricately structured as an orrery”.

Underworld by Don DeLillo (1997)

In the decade from 1982, DeLillo went on an incredible run: The Names, White Noise, Libra, Mao II. Six years of near-silence followed, broken by this 800-page epic about lives lived in the shadow of nuclear annihilation during the second half of the 20th century. Incredibly, by utilising the same elements that had made his work so distinctive – a fragmented narrative, the depiction of daily life saturated by mass media, and an atmosphere of what he refers to in an earlier novel as “accumulating dread” – he produced a sweeping, social epic of the kind few thought he had either the particular skills or the desire to write.

The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny by Kiran Desai (2025)

It gives you an idea of the scale of Desai’s novel that the lovers at its heart should meet only on page 233, just over a third of the way through the book. The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny took 20 years to write, and at one point, Desai claims, ran to 5,000 pages. Which makes the published version (688), which bounces between 1990s India and the American diaspora, and between social and magical realism, an exercise in restraint.

The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoevsky (1879-80)Vast in scope and ambition, Dostoevsky’s final novel (he died three months after its publication) unfolds over just a few days. Dmitri, Ivan and Alyosha’s occupations divide along dutiful, professional and religious lines (soldier, journalist, monk), but all of them – plus their bastard half-brother, the servant Smerdyakov – are scarred by the monstrousness of their conniving father. It’s grim, funny, savage, and possesses irresistible momentum. Other than Shakespeare, said Virginia Woolf, “there is no more exciting reading”.

A Table for Fortune by William T Vollmann (2026)

Hearing about Vollmann’s new novel, which is 3,096 pages long and costs £150, was actually the inspiration for this piece. The first two sections span the cold war, 9/11 and the “war on terror” from the point of view of a CIA analyst. The second half follows his homeless, mentally unwell son across the US. Vollmann’s longtime publisher quailed at the length of the manuscript and returned it with edits. The next time they saw it, it was 400 pages longer. He now has a new publisher. Is it worth it? I’ll tell you in about a year.

Lonesome Dove by Larry McMurtry (1985)

For mysterious reasons, numerous people have recommended this 1985 novel to me in recent years. Mysterious, that is, until I began this utterly addictive story of two friends, retired Texas Rangers, attempting the first cattle drive from the Rio Grande all the way to Montana. The journey encompasses locusts, bandits, torrential rain, kidnappings and stampedes. Punctuating these episodic adventures are haunting images of American crimes: the starving remnants of Native American tribes, pyramids of buffalo bones, and the environmental destruction wrought by the cattle industry.

A Glastonbury Romance by John Cowper Powys (1932)In very simplified terms, Powys’s chaotically structured but singular 1,200-page novel is about a conflict between two residents of the Somerset town of Glastonbury. The industrialist Philip Crow wants to exploit the land and electrify the county (even the caves of Wookey Hole), while ex-Methodist minister John Geard’s ambition is to restore Glastonbury’s status as a pilgrimage site. Powys inhabits not just the consciousnesses of his living characters but also corpses and at one point a tree. Margaret Drabble compared his achievement to Tolkein’s. Although his country is “less visited”, she wrote, “it is as compelling, and it has more air”.

Ducks, Newburyport by Lucy Ellmann (2019)

It didn’t win the Booker, but at 1,030 pages

it remains the longest novel ever shortlisted for the prize. The book consists of a single sentence unfurling from the mind of an Ohio homemaker, interrupted occasionally by an account of a mountain lioness raising her cubs. The book’s momentum is maintained by repeated use of the phrase “the fact that”, hurtling from the domestic (washing dishes) to the political (Syria, Trump) to the relatable (“the fact that I have not read all the books I want to read, not even half”).

War and Peace by Leo Tolstoy (1869)

For a long time War and Peace represented to me the stereotypical challenging long novel: to be endured more than enjoyed. When I finally read it I was surprised not only by how incredibly fun it is, but also by its many, many short chapters: 365 of them, which makes it easy to read in snatches. Yes, those snatches will go on for months, but you’ll live for them. Another surprising observation, for which Yiyun Li gets the credit: the drawing room encounters are like military campaigns and battles, while the parts about war are full of pettiness and scheming.

The Rouse by China Miéville (2026)

The winner of this year’s Goldsmiths prize, Miéville’s 1,200-page novel was two decades in the making. Over that time, he has said, “it became the defining work of my life”. It braids an evocatively described English childhood of the 1970s and 80s with the story of an occult cold war military programme to weaponise the dead, the testing ground for which lies in Britain’s dwindling colonial territories. The Rouse is a weird, glitchy, gloomy and frightening book, purposefully baffling at times, but thrilling, too.
